slides.title: 1. Direct Delivery
slides.body:
Destination on the Same Network

slides.title: 1. Direct Delivery
slides.body:
How it works?
The sender checks whether the destination IP belongs to the same network
Subnet mask is applied to both IPs to compare the network address
Sender uses ARP to find the destination's MAC address
The packet is encapsulated in a frame and sent using the MAC address

slides.title: 2. Indirect Delivery
slides.body:
Destination on a Different Network
Definition

slides.title: 2. Indirect Delivery
slides.body:
How it works?
The sender checks whether the destination IP is in a different network
If yes, the sender forwards the packet to the Default Gateway (the local router)
The router consults its Forwarding Table to determine the next hop

slides.title: 2. Indirect Delivery
slides.body:
How it works?
The packet is forwarded from router to router, hop by hop, until it reaches the destination network
The final router performs Direct Delivery to the destination host

slides.title: Next-Hop Concept
slides.body:
Key points
Hop-by-Hop
The packet moves one router at a time. Each router hands off to the next
Decentralized
Each router independently selects the next hop using its Forwarding Table
IP Header Does Not Change
The source IP and destination IP stay the same across all hops
MAC Address Changes
At each hop, the router removes the old frame and creates a new frame with new MAC addresses

slides.title: Types of NAT
slides.body:
1. Static NAT
01
One private IP permanently mapped to one public IP
The mapping is permanent and does not change
Example: 192.168.1.10 always maps to 203.0.113.10
Use case: Servers that must be reachable from the internet
Limitation: Requires one public IP per device - does not save IP addresses

slides.title: Types of NAT
slides.body:
2. Dynamic NAT
02
Private IPs share a pool of public IPs
When a private device needs internet access, it is assigned one public IP from the pool temporarily
When the session ends, the public IP returns to the pool
Limitation: If all public IPs in the pool are in use, new connections fail

3. PAT (Port Address Translation)
03
All private devices share a single public IP
Also called NAT Overload or NAPT
Port numbers are used to distinguish between different devices on the same public IP

slides.title: Types of NAT
slides.body:
3. PAT (Port Address Translation)
03
All private devices share a single public IP
Example: 192.168.1.10:1025 and 192.168.1.11:3300 both appear as 203.0.113.5 - just with different port numbers
192.168.1.10:1025 → 203.0.113.5:5001
192.168.1.11:3300 → 203.0.113.5:5002

slides.title: Types of NAT
slides.body:
PAT
03
All private devices share a single public IP
One public IP can handle up to 65,535 simultaneous connections (one per port number)
Use case: Home routers, small office routers - the most common type of NAT in use today

slides.title: NAT - Network Address Translation
slides.body:
Advantages 
Multiple devices share a single public IP, extending IPv4’s life
Internal devices are shielded, blocking unsolicited inbound traffic unless a NAT mapping exists
Changes in internal addresses don't affect the public IP

slides.title: NAT - Network Address Translation
slides.body:
Limitations
NAT prevents direct device-to-device communication, designed in the internet's architecture
Apps like VoIP and video calls struggle behind NAT, requiring workarounds (STUN/TURN)
Some apps (e.g., FTP, SIP) embed IPs in the payload, causing issues with NAT
NAT adds load by inspecting and rewriting each packet

slides.title: NAT - Network Address Translation
slides.body:
Limitations
NAT blocks unsolicited inbound traffic but doesn't inspect outbound traffic
IPv6 offers enough unique addresses, making NAT unnecessary
NAT's address rewriting complicates tracing the original traffic source
